# Probability and Statistical Foundations {#sec-probability}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives

After this chapter you should be able to:

1. define a probability space, a random variable and its distribution, and distinguish probability mass functions from probability densities;
2. derive marginal and conditional distributions from a joint distribution, and decide whether variables are independent or conditionally independent;
3. state and prove the laws of total expectation, variance and covariance, and use them to compute moments of hierarchical models;
4. derive the density of a transformed random variable, including the Jacobian factor, for monotone, non-monotone and multivariate transformations;
5. write down the likelihood of a sampling model and explain why it is not a probability density in the parameter;
6. check each of these results numerically in R and report the Monte Carlo error of the check.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Prerequisites

Calculus (including multiple integrals) and a first course in probability. No measure theory is assumed. Where it clarifies a statement it is introduced briefly, with references.
:::

## Motivation {#sec-prob-motivation}

Bayesian inference applies probability theory to unknown quantities. Every step later in the book uses the rules of this chapter. A posterior distribution is a conditional distribution. A marginal likelihood is a marginal distribution. A posterior predictive distribution is a mixture obtained by the law of total probability. A reparameterised model needs the change-of-variables formula. Many errors in applied Bayesian computation are errors in this elementary material: a missing Jacobian, a rate confused with a scale, or a likelihood treated as if it were a density in the parameter.

The chapter therefore reviews probability with the precision the rest of the book needs. We prove the results we use and check each one by simulation, because a numerical check is how a computational statistician catches algebra mistakes.

## Definitions and notation {#sec-prob-definitions}

::: {#def-probability-space}
## Probability space
A **probability space** is a triple $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ where $\Omega$ is a set of outcomes, $\mathcal F$ is a $\sigma$-algebra of subsets of $\Omega$ (the *events*: it contains $\Omega$ and is closed under complements and countable unions), and $\mathbb P:\mathcal F\to[0,1]$ is a probability measure: $\mathbb P(\Omega)=1$ and $\mathbb P(\bigcup_i A_i)=\sum_i\mathbb P(A_i)$ for pairwise disjoint events $A_1,A_2,\dots$.
:::

The $\sigma$-algebra matters for technical reasons. On $\Omega=\mathbb R$ not every subset can be assigned a length consistently, so probabilities are defined only on the Borel sets, the smallest $\sigma$-algebra containing all intervals [@billingsley1995probability, Section 3]. In this book every set we meet is a Borel set, and we will not mention $\sigma$-algebras again unless they affect a result.

::: {#def-random-variable}
## Random variable and distribution
A (real) **random variable** is a function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $\{\omega: X(\omega)\le x\}\in\mathcal F$ for every $x$. Its **distribution** is the probability measure $P_X(B)=\mathbb P(X\in B)$ on Borel sets $B$, and its **cumulative distribution function (CDF)** is $F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\le x)$. A random vector $X=(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ is a vector of random variables defined on the same space.
:::

The CDF determines the distribution. Two special cases cover almost every model in this book.

::: {#def-pmf-pdf}
## Mass and density functions
$X$ is **discrete** if it takes values in a countable set $\mathcal X$; its **probability mass function** is $p(x)=\mathbb P(X=x)$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p(x)=1$. $X$ is **(absolutely) continuous** if there is a function $p\ge0$ with $F_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x p(u)\,du$ for all $x$; $p$ is its **probability density function**, and $\mathbb P(X\in B)=\int_B p(u)\,du$.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## A density is not a probability
For continuous $X$, $\mathbb P(X=x)=0$ for every $x$. The value $p(x)$ is a probability *per unit length*: $\mathbb P(x<X\le x+h)\approx p(x)h$ for small $h$. Densities can exceed one (the $\mathrm{Beta}(20,20)$ density at $1/2$ is about $5.0$), and a density value changes when the variable is rescaled. Probability masses do neither.
:::

The two cases can be unified. A mass function is a density with respect to counting measure, and an ordinary density is a density with respect to Lebesgue measure; the Radon–Nikodym theorem makes this precise [@billingsley1995probability, Section 32]. We use the unified view in @sec-mh, where the Metropolis–Hastings ratio must compare densities with respect to a *common* reference measure.

## Mathematical development {#sec-prob-development}

### Joint, marginal and conditional distributions {#sec-prob-joint}

Let $(X,Y)$ have joint density (or mass function) $p(x,y)$. The **marginal** densities are obtained by integrating (summing) out the other variable,
$$
p(x)=\int p(x,y)\,dy,\qquad p(y)=\int p(x,y)\,dx,
$$ {#eq-marginal}
and, wherever $p(x)>0$, the **conditional** density of $Y$ given $X=x$ is
$$
p(y\mid x)=\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)}.
$$ {#eq-conditional}
For fixed $x$, @eq-conditional is a density in $y$: it is non-negative and integrates to $p(x)/p(x)=1$. Rearranging gives the **product rule** $p(x,y)=p(x)\,p(y\mid x)=p(y)\,p(x\mid y)$, and equating the two factorisations gives **Bayes' rule for densities**,
$$
p(x\mid y)=\frac{p(y\mid x)\,p(x)}{p(y)}=\frac{p(y\mid x)\,p(x)}{\int p(y\mid u)\,p(u)\,du}.
$$ {#eq-bayes-densities}
With $x$ replaced by a parameter $\theta$ and $y$ by data, this is the formula on which the whole of Part II rests (@sec-bayes-paradigm).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Conditioning on events of probability zero
For continuous $X$, @eq-conditional conditions on the event $\{X=x\}$, which has probability zero. The conditional density is defined only up to sets of $x$ of probability zero, and different limiting procedures can give different "conditional distributions" given the same null event. This is the Borel–Kolmogorov paradox [@billingsley1995probability, Section 33]. In practice we always condition on a *random variable* through a fixed joint density, which removes the ambiguity. @exr-prob-10 explores the paradox.
:::

### Independence and conditional independence {#sec-prob-independence}

::: {#def-independence}
## Independence
$X$ and $Y$ are **independent** if $p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)$ for all $(x,y)$, equivalently $p(y\mid x)=p(y)$ wherever $p(x)>0$. They are **conditionally independent given $Z$**, written $X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y\mid Z$, if $p(x,y\mid z)=p(x\mid z)\,p(y\mid z)$ for all $x,y$ and all $z$ with $p(z)>0$.
:::

Conditional independence is the basic structural assumption of statistical models. "Observations $y_1,\dots,y_n$ are independent given $\theta$" means
$$
p(y_1,\dots,y_n\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i\mid\theta).
$$ {#eq-iid-given-theta}
It does **not** mean the observations are independent once $\theta$ is unknown. In a Bayesian model $\theta$ is random, and averaging over it creates dependence:

::: {#prp-ci-not-independence}
## Conditional independence does not imply independence
Let $Y_1, Y_2$ be conditionally independent given $\Lambda$, with $\mathbb E[Y_i\mid\Lambda]=m(\Lambda)$ for $i=1,2$, and suppose $\operatorname{Var}\{m(\Lambda)\}$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y_i^2]$ are finite. Then $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)=\operatorname{Var}\{m(\Lambda)\}$. In particular $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ are positively correlated, hence dependent, whenever $m(\Lambda)$ is non-degenerate.
:::

::: {.proof}
By the law of total covariance (@thm-total-variance), $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)=\mathbb E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2\mid\Lambda)]+\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb E[Y_1\mid\Lambda],\mathbb E[Y_2\mid\Lambda])$. Conditional independence makes the first term zero, and the second is $\operatorname{Cov}(m(\Lambda),m(\Lambda))=\operatorname{Var}\{m(\Lambda)\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Intuition
If two coins come from the same mint and the mint's bias is unknown, a head on the first coin is evidence that the bias favours heads, which raises the probability of a head on the second. The tosses are independent *given* the bias and dependent *marginally*. This is exactly how Bayesian models "learn": observed data change our predictions for unobserved data through the shared parameter.
:::

### Expectation, variance and covariance {#sec-prob-moments}

For a function $g$, the **expectation** of $g(X)$ is $\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int g(x)\,p(x)\,dx$, provided $\int\lvert g(x)\rvert p(x)\,dx<\infty$. If this integral diverges the expectation does not exist. This is not a technicality: the Cauchy distribution has no mean, and several estimators in later chapters (notably importance sampling in @sec-importance) fail precisely because a variance is infinite. Expectation is linear: $\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\mathbb E[X]+b\mathbb E[Y]$ whenever both expectations exist, with no independence required.

The **variance** is $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb EX)^2]=\mathbb E[X^2]-(\mathbb EX)^2$, the **covariance** is $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb EX)(Y-\mathbb EY)]$, and the **correlation** is $\operatorname{Cor}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}X\operatorname{Var}Y}$. For a random vector $X\in\mathbb R^d$ the covariance matrix $\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^\top]$ has entries $\Sigma_{jk}=\operatorname{Cov}(X_j,X_k)$, and for a fixed matrix $A$, $\operatorname{Cov}(AX)=A\Sigma A^\top$.

::: {#prp-correlation-bound}
## Correlation lies in $[-1,1]$
If $0<\operatorname{Var}X,\operatorname{Var}Y<\infty$ then $\lvert\operatorname{Cor}(X,Y)\rvert\le1$, with equality if and only if $Y=a+bX$ almost surely for constants $a$ and $b\neq0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $U=X-\mathbb EX$, $V=Y-\mathbb EY$. For every real $t$, $0\le\mathbb E[(V-tU)^2]=\operatorname{Var}Y-2t\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)+t^2\operatorname{Var}X$. A quadratic in $t$ that is non-negative everywhere has non-positive discriminant: $4\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2-4\operatorname{Var}X\operatorname{Var}Y\le0$, which is the claim. Equality holds if and only if the quadratic has a real root $t^\star$, that is $\mathbb E[(V-t^\star U)^2]=0$, i.e. $V=t^\star U$ almost surely.
:::

Zero correlation does not imply independence (@exr-prob-5). Correlation measures *linear* dependence only.

### Conditional expectation and the laws of total expectation and variance {#sec-prob-conditional-expectation}

For jointly distributed $(X,Y)$, the **conditional expectation** of $Y$ given $X=x$ is $\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=\int y\,p(y\mid x)\,dy$. As a function of $x$ this is a fixed function $m(x)$, and $\mathbb E[Y\mid X]$ denotes the *random variable* $m(X)$. The conditional variance $\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)$ is defined in the same way.

::: {#thm-tower}
## Law of total expectation (tower property)
If $\mathbb E\lvert Y\rvert<\infty$, then $\mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\big]=\mathbb E[Y]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For jointly continuous variables with density $p(x,y)$ (the discrete case replaces integrals by sums),
$$
\mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\big]=\int\Big(\int y\,p(y\mid x)\,dy\Big)p(x)\,dx=\iint y\,p(x,y)\,dy\,dx=\mathbb E[Y],
$$
where exchanging the order of integration is justified by Fubini's theorem because $\iint\lvert y\rvert p(x,y)\,dy\,dx=\mathbb E\lvert Y\rvert<\infty$.
:::

::: {#thm-total-variance}
## Laws of total variance and covariance
If $\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty$ then
$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E\big[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)\big]+\operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\big).
$$ {#eq-total-variance}
More generally, if $\mathbb E[Y^2],\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty$, then $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)=\mathbb E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)]+\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbb E[Y\mid X],\mathbb E[Z\mid X])$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove the covariance identity; the variance identity is the case $Z=Y$. Write $m_Y(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X]$ and $m_Z(X)=\mathbb E[Z\mid X]$. By definition, $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)=\mathbb E[YZ\mid X]-m_Y(X)m_Z(X)$. Taking expectations and applying @thm-tower to $YZ$ (integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz),
$$
\mathbb E[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)]=\mathbb E[YZ]-\mathbb E[m_Y(X)m_Z(X)].
$$
Also, using @thm-tower twice, $\operatorname{Cov}(m_Y(X),m_Z(X))=\mathbb E[m_Y(X)m_Z(X)]-\mathbb E[Y]\mathbb E[Z]$. Adding the two displays gives $\mathbb E[YZ]-\mathbb E[Y]\mathbb E[Z]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Intuition
@eq-total-variance splits uncertainty about $Y$ into the average uncertainty that remains once $X$ is known, plus the uncertainty that comes from not knowing $X$. In Bayesian prediction (@sec-prediction) the same decomposition splits predictive variance into "noise" and "parameter uncertainty". The second part shrinks as data accumulate; the first does not.
:::

### Transformations of random variables {#sec-prob-transformations}

Reparameterisation is everywhere in Bayesian computation. Samplers work better on unconstrained scales, so a positive scale parameter $\sigma$ is often sampled as $\log\sigma$. Getting the density of the new parameter right requires the change-of-variables formula.

::: {#thm-change-of-variables}
## Change of variables
Let $X$ have density $p_X$ on an open set $\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $g:\mathcal U\to\mathcal V$ be a bijection onto an open set $\mathcal V$, continuously differentiable with continuously differentiable inverse $h=g^{-1}$. Then $Y=g(X)$ has density
$$
p_Y(y)=p_X\big(h(y)\big)\,\big\lvert\det J_h(y)\big\rvert,\qquad y\in\mathcal V,
$$ {#eq-change-of-variables}
where $J_h(y)=\partial h(y)/\partial y$ is the Jacobian matrix of the inverse map. In one dimension, $p_Y(y)=p_X(h(y))\,\lvert h'(y)\rvert$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove the one-dimensional case with $g$ increasing; the decreasing case is identical up to a sign, and the multivariate case follows from the change-of-variables theorem for multiple integrals [@billingsley1995probability, Theorem 17.2]. For $y\in\mathcal V$, $F_Y(y)=\mathbb P(g(X)\le y)=\mathbb P(X\le h(y))=F_X(h(y))$ because $g$ is increasing. Differentiating with the chain rule gives $p_Y(y)=p_X(h(y))\,h'(y)$, and $h'(y)=\lvert h'(y)\rvert$ because $h$ is increasing.
:::

If $g$ is not one-to-one, split its domain into pieces on which it is, apply @eq-change-of-variables on each piece, and add the results (@exr-prob-3).

::: {#exm-lognormal}
## Log-normal distribution
If $X\sim\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and $Y=e^X$, then $h(y)=\log y$ and $h'(y)=1/y$, so
$p_Y(y)=\frac{1}{y\sigma}\phi\big(\frac{\log y-\mu}{\sigma}\big)$ for $y>0$. The factor $1/y$ is the Jacobian. Without it, $p_Y$ would not integrate to one.
:::

::: {#exm-log-scale-prior}
## A prior on the log scale
Suppose $\sigma\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ and we sample $\eta=\log\sigma$. Then $\sigma=h(\eta)=e^\eta$, $h'(\eta)=e^\eta$, and
$p_\eta(\eta)=e^{-e^\eta}\,e^{\eta}$. The extra $e^\eta$, or $+\eta$ on the log scale, is the "log-Jacobian adjustment" that appears in every sampler that works on transformed parameters, including Stan [@stan2026reference] and our own hierarchical models (`R/models/hierarchical.R`).
:::

### Common distributions and their parameterisations {#sec-prob-distributions}

The distributions used in this book, with the parameterisations fixed on the [notation page](../front/notation.qmd), are listed in full in [Appendix A](../appendices/distributions.qmd). Three facts are worth stating here because they recur.

1. **Rate versus scale.** $\mathrm{Gamma}(a,b)$ with rate $b$ has mean $a/b$; with scale $b$ it has mean $ab$. R's `dgamma(x, shape, rate)` uses the rate if you name it, but its *third positional argument* is `rate`, so `dgamma(x, 2, 3)` means rate 3. Name the argument.
2. **Variance versus standard deviation.** We write $\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with the variance, while R's `dnorm(x, mean, sd)` takes the standard deviation.
3. **Exponential families.** Many standard laws have densities of the form $p(y\mid\theta)=h(y)\exp\{\eta(\theta)^\top T(y)-A(\theta)\}$. For these, the likelihood of $n$ independent observations depends on the data only through $\sum_i T(y_i)$, a *sufficient statistic*. This is why conjugate priors exist for them (@sec-conjugate) [@diaconis1979conjugate].

### Likelihood functions and sampling models {#sec-prob-likelihood}

A **sampling model** (or *data-generating model*) is a family of distributions $\{p(y\mid\theta):\theta\in\Theta\}$ for the data. Once data $y$ are observed, the same formula read as a function of $\theta$ is the likelihood.

::: {#def-likelihood}
## Likelihood
For observed data $y$, the **likelihood function** is $L(\theta;y)=p(y\mid\theta)$, viewed as a function of $\theta\in\Theta$ with $y$ held fixed. The **log-likelihood** is $\ell(\theta)=\log L(\theta;y)$. Under @eq-iid-given-theta, $\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p(y_i\mid\theta)$.
:::

The likelihood is **not** a probability density for $\theta$: nothing makes $\int L(\theta;y)\,d\theta$ equal to one, or even finite. For $y$ successes in $n$ binomial trials, $\int_0^1\binom ny\theta^y(1-\theta)^{n-y}\,d\theta=1/(n+1)$ (@exr-prob-9). Turning a likelihood into a distribution over $\theta$ requires a prior and normalisation, which is Bayes' rule @eq-bayes-densities. The likelihood is also defined only up to factors that do not depend on $\theta$. Such factors cancel in every likelihood ratio and in every posterior.

::: {.callout-note}
## Random variable, realisation, parameter
Three different kinds of object appear in a statistical model and are easy to confuse:

- a **random variable** $Y_i$ is a function on the outcome space, and the model assigns it a distribution;
- a **realisation** $y_i$ is the number actually observed: a fixed constant once the data are in hand;
- a **parameter** $\theta$ indexes the family of distributions. In frequentist inference it is an unknown constant. In Bayesian inference it is *also* modelled as a random variable, with a prior distribution, and inference conditions on the realisations.

The likelihood is a function of the parameter evaluated at fixed realisations. A sampling distribution is a distribution of the random variables at a fixed parameter. A posterior is a distribution of the parameter given fixed realisations.
:::

## Worked example: a two-stage count model {#sec-prob-worked}

Consider the hierarchical model
$$
\Lambda\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(a,b),\qquad Y_1,Y_2\mid\Lambda\ \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}\ \mathrm{Poisson}(\Lambda),
$$
with shape $a>0$ and rate $b>0$. It describes, for example, counts from two periods of a process with an unknown underlying rate. We derive its marginal distribution, moments, dependence and a conditional distribution, using only this chapter's tools.

**Step 1: the marginal distribution of one count.** By @eq-marginal, for $y\in\{0,1,\dots\}$,
$$
p(y)=\int_0^\infty\frac{\lambda^ye^{-\lambda}}{y!}\cdot\frac{b^a\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}}{\Gamma(a)}\,d\lambda
=\frac{b^a}{y!\,\Gamma(a)}\int_0^\infty\lambda^{a+y-1}e^{-(b+1)\lambda}\,d\lambda
=\frac{\Gamma(a+y)}{\Gamma(a)\,y!}\Big(\frac{b}{b+1}\Big)^a\Big(\frac{1}{b+1}\Big)^y,
$$
where we used $\int_0^\infty\lambda^{c-1}e^{-d\lambda}\,d\lambda=\Gamma(c)/d^c$. This is the **negative binomial** distribution with size $a$ and success probability $b/(b+1)$ (`dnbinom(y, size = a, prob = b / (b + 1))` in R).

**Step 2: moments by the total laws.** Since $\mathbb E[Y\mid\Lambda]=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\Lambda)=\Lambda$, @thm-tower and @thm-total-variance give
$$
\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[\Lambda]=\frac ab,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E[\Lambda]+\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda)=\frac ab+\frac a{b^2}.
$$
The marginal variance exceeds the mean (*overdispersion*). The extra $a/b^2$ comes entirely from not knowing $\Lambda$.

**Step 3: dependence.** By @prp-ci-not-independence with $m(\Lambda)=\Lambda$, $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_1,Y_2)=\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda)=a/b^2$, so
$\operatorname{Cor}(Y_1,Y_2)=\dfrac{a/b^2}{a/b+a/b^2}=\dfrac{1}{b+1}.$

**Step 4: what the first count says about the rate.** By @eq-bayes-densities,
$$
p(\lambda\mid y_1)\propto\frac{\lambda^{y_1}e^{-\lambda}}{y_1!}\cdot\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}\propto\lambda^{a+y_1-1}e^{-(b+1)\lambda},
$$
which is the kernel of $\mathrm{Gamma}(a+y_1,\,b+1)$. The first observation updates the distribution of the rate, and through it the prediction for $Y_2$. This is a first instance of the conjugate updating developed in @sec-conjugate.

## R implementation {#sec-prob-r}

R provides four functions for each standard distribution: `d*` (density or mass), `p*` (CDF), `q*` (quantile) and `r*` (random generation). The code below checks the worked example by simulating the two-stage model directly: draw $\Lambda$, then draw $Y_1,Y_2$ given $\Lambda$.

```{r}
#| label: prob-simulate-two-stage
a <- 3; b <- 0.5            # Gamma(shape 3, rate 0.5): E[Lambda] = 6
n_sim <- 1e5
set.seed(101)
lambda <- rgamma(n_sim, shape = a, rate = b)      # name the rate argument!
y1 <- rpois(n_sim, lambda)
y2 <- rpois(n_sim, lambda)                        # same Lambda: conditionally iid

c(mean_sim = mean(y1), mean_exact = a / b,
  var_sim = var(y1), var_exact = a / b + a / b^2,
  cor_sim = cor(y1, y2), cor_exact = 1 / (b + 1))
```

The marginal pmf from Step 1 can be compared with the simulated frequencies:

```{r}
#| label: prob-marginal-check
k <- 0:25
freq_sim <- as.vector(table(factor(y1, levels = k))) / n_sim
pmf_exact <- dnbinom(k, size = a, prob = b / (b + 1))
# Monte Carlo standard error of a simulated frequency: sqrt(p (1 - p) / n)
mcse <- sqrt(pmf_exact * (1 - pmf_exact) / n_sim)
head(data.frame(k, freq_sim, pmf_exact, z = (freq_sim - pmf_exact) / mcse), 8)
```

The column `z` is the discrepancy measured in Monte Carlo standard errors. For a correct derivation these are roughly standard normal, so values of size 1 or 2 are expected and values beyond 4 indicate an error.

## Computational experiment: transformations and the Jacobian {#sec-prob-experiment}

We check @thm-change-of-variables numerically in two cases: the log-normal of @exm-lognormal, and a non-monotone map $Y=X^2$ with $X\sim\mathrm N(0,1)$, whose density is the $\chi^2_1$ density $p_Y(y)=(2\pi y)^{-1/2}e^{-y/2}$ (@exr-prob-3).

```{r}
#| label: fig-prob-jacobian
#| fig-cap: "Simulated draws of transformed variables (histograms) against densities from the change-of-variables formula (orange). Left: $Y=e^X$ with $X\\sim\\mathrm{N}(0,0.5^2)$. Right: $Y=X^2$ with $X\\sim\\mathrm N(0,1)$, which needs two branches of the inverse."
#| fig-height: 3.6
set.seed(102)
x <- rnorm(2e5, 0, 0.5)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist_density(exp(x), function(y) dnorm(log(y), 0, 0.5) / y, breaks = 80,
             xlab = "y = exp(x)", xlim = c(0, 4))
curve(dnorm(log(x), 0, 0.5), add = TRUE, lty = 2, col = course_muted)   # Jacobian omitted
legend("topright", c("with Jacobian", "without"), lty = c(1, 2),
       col = c(course_cols[["orange"]], course_muted), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
z <- rnorm(2e5)^2
hist_density(z[z < 6], function(y) dchisq(y, 1) / pchisq(6, 1), breaks = 120,
             xlab = "y = x^2 (truncated at 6)")
```

The dashed curve shows what you get if the Jacobian factor $1/y$ is forgotten. It is not a density, and it disagrees with the simulation. Checking against simulation catches this kind of algebra error immediately.

A sharper check than a picture uses probabilities of intervals, each with a Monte Carlo standard error:

```{r}
#| label: prob-interval-check
breaks <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, Inf)
p_exact <- diff(plnorm(breaks, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 0.5))   # exact interval probabilities
p_sim <- as.vector(table(cut(exp(x), breaks))) / length(x)
round(cbind(p_exact, p_sim, z = (p_sim - p_exact) / sqrt(p_exact * (1 - p_exact) / length(x))), 4)
```

## Diagnostics and validation {#sec-prob-validation}

The checks above follow a pattern used throughout the book.

1. **Derive** the quantity analytically: a pmf, a moment, a density.
2. **Simulate** from the generative model *as written*, not from the derived result. Otherwise the check is circular.
3. **Compare** with a tolerance set by Monte Carlo error, not by eye. For an estimated probability $\hat p$ from $n$ independent draws, the standard error is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. For a sample mean it is $s/\sqrt n$. Discrepancies are reported in standard errors.
4. **Vary** the seed and the parameter values. A derivation that is correct for $a=3,b=0.5$ but wrong in general shows up as a failure for other values.

A global test such as a $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test can combine many cells. Keep in mind that with $10^5$ draws such tests detect differences far too small to matter, and with $10^2$ draws they miss large ones. The size of the discrepancy, in standard errors, is more informative than a p-value.

```{r}
#| label: prob-chisq
obs <- table(factor(pmin(y1, 25), levels = 0:25))
p_cells <- c(dnbinom(0:24, size = a, prob = b / (b + 1)),
             pnbinom(24, size = a, prob = b / (b + 1), lower.tail = FALSE))  # last cell: 25+
chisq.test(as.vector(obs), p = p_cells)$p.value
```

## Interpretation {#sec-prob-interpretation}

The worked example is the simplest *hierarchical* model, and its properties carry over to the large models of @sec-hierarchical. Marginalising over an unknown rate turned independent Poisson counts into dependent, overdispersed negative-binomial counts. Conditioning on an observed count turned a Gamma prior into a Gamma posterior. Both effects come from @eq-marginal and @eq-conditional; nothing specifically "Bayesian" was needed beyond treating $\Lambda$ as random.

## Limitations and common errors {#sec-prob-errors}

- **Reading a density value as a probability.** $p(x)=3$ is not an error; $\mathbb P(X=x)=3$ is.
- **Forgetting the Jacobian.** Any change of variables in a density, including for priors on transformed parameters, needs @eq-change-of-variables. Leaving it out changes the model, not merely its parameterisation.
- **Confusing rate and scale, or variance and standard deviation.** Check every call to `dgamma`, `rgamma`, `dnorm` and `rnorm` against the notation page.
- **Treating zero correlation as independence.** Only for jointly Gaussian vectors are the two equivalent.
- **Treating conditional independence as independence.** Observations that are independent given $\theta$ are, in general, dependent marginally (@prp-ci-not-independence).
- **Integrating a likelihood as if it were a density in $\theta$.** It generally does not integrate to one. Normalisation requires a prior.
- **Assuming moments exist.** Heavy-tailed distributions may lack a mean or variance, and then sample averages do not settle down.

## Chapter summary {#sec-prob-summary}

- A distribution assigns probabilities to events. Mass functions give probabilities of points; densities give probabilities per unit length and integrate to probabilities.
- Marginals integrate out variables, conditionals divide by marginals, and the product rule combined with marginalisation yields Bayes' rule for densities (@eq-bayes-densities).
- Conditional independence given a parameter is the core assumption of statistical models. It does not imply marginal independence.
- The laws of total expectation, variance and covariance (@thm-tower, @thm-total-variance) decompose moments of hierarchical models.
- Transforming a continuous variable multiplies its density by the absolute Jacobian of the inverse map (@thm-change-of-variables).
- The likelihood is the sampling density read as a function of the parameter. It is not a density for the parameter.

## Exercises {#sec-prob-exercises}

::: {#exr-prob-1}
**[Conceptual ★]** A clinical trial records whether each of $n=40$ patients responds to a treatment, and the analyst models the responses as $Y_i\mid\theta\stackrel{\text{iid}}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\theta)$. Identify the random variables, the realisations and the parameter. Which of them are random in a Bayesian analysis, and which in a frequentist analysis?
:::

::: {#exr-prob-2}
**[Mathematical ★]** Let $X$ have density $p(x)=2x$ on $(0,1)$. Verify that $p$ is a density, compute $F_X$, $\mathbb E[X]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, and find the density of $Y=-\log X$.
:::

::: {#exr-prob-3}
**[Mathematical ★★]** Let $X\sim\mathrm N(0,1)$ and $Y=X^2$. The map $x\mapsto x^2$ is not one-to-one on $\mathbb R$. Derive the density of $Y$ by splitting $\mathbb R$ into $(-\infty,0)$ and $(0,\infty)$, and show it equals the $\chi^2_1$ density.
:::

::: {#exr-prob-4}
**[Proof ★★]** Prove the law of total variance @eq-total-variance directly (without the covariance identity), stating where finiteness of $\mathbb E[Y^2]$ is used.
:::

::: {#exr-prob-5}
**[Proof ★]** Let $X\sim\mathrm N(0,1)$ and $Y=X^2$. Show that $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0$ but $X$ and $Y$ are not independent.
:::

::: {#exr-prob-6}
**[Mathematical ★★]** Let $\theta\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ and $Y\mid\theta\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\theta)$. (a) Derive the marginal mass function of $Y$ (the *beta-binomial* distribution). (b) Use the total laws to compute $\mathbb E[Y]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$, and compare $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ with the binomial variance $n\bar\theta(1-\bar\theta)$, $\bar\theta=\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$.
:::

::: {#exr-prob-7}
**[R ★]** Simulate $10^5$ draws of $(X,X^2)$ with $X\sim\mathrm N(0,1)$. Estimate $\operatorname{Cor}(X,X^2)$ and $\operatorname{Cor}(\lvert X\rvert,X^2)$, each with a standard error obtained by repeating the simulation 200 times. What does this tell you about using correlation to detect dependence?
:::

::: {#exr-prob-8}
**[Simulation ★★]** Using the course function `beta_binomial_update()` and `dbetabinom_log()` from `R/models/conjugate.R`, verify your answer to @exr-prob-6(a) by simulating the two-stage model for $\alpha=2,\beta=5,n=12$. Report the largest discrepancy in Monte Carlo standard errors across all values of $y$.
:::

::: {#exr-prob-9}
**[Mathematical ★]** Show that $\int_0^1\binom ny\theta^y(1-\theta)^{n-y}\,d\theta=1/(n+1)$ for every $y\in\{0,\dots,n\}$. Interpret this as a statement about the marginal distribution of $Y$ under a uniform prior on $\theta$.
:::

::: {#exr-prob-10}
**[Research ★★★]** (Borel–Kolmogorov.) Let a point be uniform on the unit sphere. Compute the conditional distribution of its longitude given that it lies on the equator, and the conditional distribution of its latitude given that it lies on a fixed meridian, each as a limit of conditioning on thin bands. Explain why the two answers are inconsistent with "uniform on a great circle", and what this implies for defining conditional densities on events of probability zero.
:::

## Further reading {#sec-prob-reading}

- @casella2002inference, Chapters 1–4: a careful treatment of distributions, transformations and conditional expectation at the level of this chapter.
- @billingsley1995probability and @durrett2019probability: measure-theoretic probability, including Radon–Nikodym derivatives and regular conditional distributions.
- @williams1991martingales: an elegant account of conditional expectation as a projection.
- @wasserman2004all, Chapters 1–3: a concise review aimed at statisticians.
- @diaconis1979conjugate: the exponential-family structure behind conjugate priors.

## Solutions {#sec-prob-solutions}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-1
The random variables are $Y_1,\dots,Y_{40}$, the patients' responses as functions on the outcome space. The realisations are the observed $0/1$ values $y_1,\dots,y_{40}$. The parameter is the response probability $\theta$. In a frequentist analysis only the $Y_i$ are random; $\theta$ is an unknown constant, and probability statements describe the behaviour of procedures over hypothetical repetitions of the trial. In a Bayesian analysis $\theta$ is also given a distribution (the prior), and inference is the conditional distribution of $\theta$ given the realisations.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-2
$p\ge0$ and $\int_0^1 2x\,dx=1$. $F_X(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$. $\mathbb E X=\int_0^1 2x^2dx=2/3$, $\mathbb E X^2=\int_0^12x^3dx=1/2$, so $\operatorname{Var}X=1/2-4/9=1/18$. For $Y=-\log X$, $h(y)=e^{-y}$, $\lvert h'(y)\rvert=e^{-y}$, and $p_Y(y)=2e^{-y}\cdot e^{-y}=2e^{-2y}$ for $y>0$: $Y\sim\mathrm{Exp}(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-3
On $(0,\infty)$ the inverse is $h_+(y)=\sqrt y$ and on $(-\infty,0)$ it is $h_-(y)=-\sqrt y$; both have $\lvert h'(y)\rvert=1/(2\sqrt y)$. For $y>0$, $\mathbb P(Y\le y)=\mathbb P(-\sqrt y\le X\le\sqrt y)$, and differentiating, $p_Y(y)=\phi(\sqrt y)\frac1{2\sqrt y}+\phi(-\sqrt y)\frac1{2\sqrt y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}e^{-y/2}$, the $\chi^2_1$ density $\frac{1}{2^{1/2}\Gamma(1/2)}y^{-1/2}e^{-y/2}$ since $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-4
Let $m(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X]$. Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)=\mathbb E[Y^2\mid X]-m(X)^2$, so by @thm-tower applied to $Y^2$ (integrable by assumption), $\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]=\mathbb E[Y^2]-\mathbb E[m(X)^2]$. Also $\operatorname{Var}(m(X))=\mathbb E[m(X)^2]-(\mathbb E[m(X)])^2=\mathbb E[m(X)^2]-(\mathbb EY)^2$. Adding gives $\mathbb E[Y^2]-(\mathbb EY)^2=\operatorname{Var}Y$. Finiteness of $\mathbb E[Y^2]$ guarantees that all terms are finite, since $\mathbb E[m(X)^2]\le\mathbb E[Y^2]$ by conditional Jensen, so no $\infty-\infty$ arises.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-5
$\operatorname{Cov}(X,X^2)=\mathbb E[X^3]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[X^2]=0-0=0$ because odd moments of $\mathrm N(0,1)$ vanish. But $\mathbb P(Y\le1\mid\lvert X\rvert>1)=0\neq\mathbb P(Y\le1)\approx0.683$, so the conditional distribution of $Y$ depends on $X$ and they are dependent. Indeed $Y$ is a deterministic function of $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-6
(a) $p(y)=\int_0^1\binom ny\theta^y(1-\theta)^{n-y}\frac{\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}d\theta=\binom ny\frac{B(y+\alpha,n-y+\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}$, $y=0,\dots,n$.
(b) $\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[n\theta]=n\bar\theta$. $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E[n\theta(1-\theta)]+\operatorname{Var}(n\theta)$. With $\operatorname{Var}\theta=\bar\theta(1-\bar\theta)/(\alpha+\beta+1)$ and $\mathbb E[\theta(1-\theta)]=\bar\theta-\operatorname{Var}\theta-\bar\theta^2=\bar\theta(1-\bar\theta)\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+1}$,
$$\operatorname{Var}(Y)=n\bar\theta(1-\bar\theta)\Big[\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha+\beta+1}+\frac{n}{\alpha+\beta+1}\Big]=n\bar\theta(1-\bar\theta)\frac{\alpha+\beta+n}{\alpha+\beta+1},$$
which exceeds the binomial variance by the factor $(\alpha+\beta+n)/(\alpha+\beta+1)\ge1$ (equality only when $n=1$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-7
A possible solution:
```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1)
reps <- replicate(200, { x <- rnorm(1e5); c(cor(x, x^2), cor(abs(x), x^2)) })
rowMeans(reps); apply(reps, 1, sd)
```
$\operatorname{Cor}(X,X^2)$ is about $0\pm0.003$, while $\operatorname{Cor}(\lvert X\rvert,X^2)\approx0.97$. Correlation only detects the dependence it is "aimed at": the same dependence is invisible to one statistic and obvious to another. Checking dependence requires either several functions of the variables or a direct comparison of conditional distributions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-8
```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(2)
al <- 2; be <- 5; n <- 12; S <- 2e5
y <- rbinom(S, n, rbeta(S, al, be))
p_exact <- exp(dbetabinom_log(0:n, n, al, be))
p_sim <- tabulate(y + 1, nbins = n + 1) / S
max(abs(p_sim - p_exact) / sqrt(p_exact * (1 - p_exact) / S))
```
The maximum absolute $z$-score over the 13 cells should typically be below about 3. Values above 4 indicate an error in the derivation or the code.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-9
$\int_0^1\theta^y(1-\theta)^{n-y}d\theta=B(y+1,n-y+1)=\frac{y!\,(n-y)!}{(n+1)!}$, so the integral equals $\binom ny\frac{y!(n-y)!}{(n+1)!}=\frac1{n+1}$. Under $\theta\sim\mathrm U(0,1)$ the integral is exactly the marginal probability $\mathbb P(Y=y)$, so the marginal distribution of $Y$ is uniform on $\{0,\dots,n\}$, which is Bayes' own argument for the uniform prior [@bayes1763essay]. As a function of $\theta$ for fixed $y$, the likelihood integrates to $1/(n+1)$, not one: it is not a density in $\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to @exr-prob-10
Use longitude $\lambda\in[0,2\pi)$ and latitude $\varphi\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$; the uniform distribution on the sphere has density $\cos\varphi/(4\pi)$ in $(\lambda,\varphi)$. Conditioning on the band $\lvert\varphi\rvert<\epsilon$ and letting $\epsilon\to0$ gives longitude uniform on the equator. Conditioning on the wedge $\lvert\lambda-\lambda_0\rvert<\epsilon$ (together with its antipodal wedge, to obtain a full great circle) gives a latitude density proportional to $\cos\varphi$, not uniform, because the wedge is wider near the equator than near the poles. Both circles are great circles, and by symmetry one would expect a uniform answer on each. The resolution is that "the conditional distribution given a null event" is not defined by the event alone. It depends on the random variable (the $\sigma$-algebra) being conditioned on, here $\varphi$ versus $\lambda$. Conditional densities are therefore always defined relative to a specified joint density and conditioning variable, as in @eq-conditional.
:::
